analysis.one_liner: Orders the Treasury Department to break up banks and insurers too big to fail.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee in April 2013, received no cosponsors, and never got a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Treasury Secretary to list every commercial bank, investment bank, hedge fund, and insurance company it considered too big to fail, then break up each one so its collapse could no longer wreck the economy or force a taxpayer bailout. It was the legislative version of the argument that no financial institution should be so large that the government has to rescue it.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who since the 2008 crisis have been the backstop when giant financial firms get into trouble; the bill aimed to remove that risk by eliminating the firms that create it. Smaller banks and credit unions would also have faced less distortion from competitors that are effectively guaranteed government rescue.

how_it_helps.text: Within 90 days of enactment, the Treasury Secretary would have had to submit to Congress a list of all commercial banks, investment banks, hedge funds, and insurance companies believed to be too big to fail, including U.S. bank holding companies identified as systemically important by the Financial Stability Board.

Starting one year after enactment, the Treasury Secretary would have been required to break up every institution on that list so that its failure would no longer cause a catastrophic effect on the U.S. or global economy without a taxpayer bailout.

analysis.who_pays: The largest U.S. banks, investment banks, hedge funds, and insurance companies, whose current size gives them cheaper borrowing and a competitive edge because markets expect a government rescue. Their shareholders and executives would bear the cost of forced breakups.

drawbacks.text: The bill gave the Treasury Secretary broad discretion: the only standard for making the list is that an entity is so large its failure would have catastrophic effects without government assistance, and the text sets no detailed instructions for how or into what pieces institutions should be broken up.

The one-year deadline would have forced a sweeping restructuring of the largest financial institutions on a very short timeline, a disruption even supporters of breaking up big banks debated how to carry out.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The goal — no financial firm so big its collapse forces a taxpayer rescue — addresses a real public risk made plain by the 2008 crisis. The design is blunt, though: it hands the Treasury Secretary one year and broad discretion to dismantle some of the world's largest financial institutions without laying out the mechanics, so implementation would have been contentious even if it had moved.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on April 9, 2013.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day; that was the last action of any kind recorded.
The Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs never held a hearing or vote on the bill, and it was never reported to the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest systemically important banks, insurers, and hedge funds, which kept their size and the market expectation of government rescue, since the bill never advanced and they faced no breakup requirement.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its call to list and break up too-big-to-fail institutions.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never held a hearing or vote or reported the bill; it died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Independent sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan bloc ever took a recorded position on it.

industries.note: The bill would have forced banks whose failure could crash the economy to be broken up, ending the implicit government guarantee that lowers their borrowing costs. That guarantee is effectively a public subsidy funded by ordinary taxpayers as potential bailers-out.

industries.industry: Large investment banks and hedge funds
industries.note: The bill's list was required to include investment banks and hedge funds deemed too big to fail, and it would have required their breakup as well.
Too-big-to-fail insurers were explicitly on the list of entities the Treasury Secretary would have had to break up.
Competitors that were previously seen as guaranteed government rescue would lose that edge, leveling the playing field for smaller institutions.
